solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Sell-out of English carrier absorbed in BA deal finally

indicators.note: what is absorbed in something is taken inside it

parts.note: BA, printed in capitals, gives its two letters and holds the rest

indicators.note: points to the last letter of the word before it

explanation.surface: A newspaper cries betrayal over a British Airways takeover deal that swallowed an English airline.
explanation.walkthrough: BA and 'carrier' pull hard toward airlines, but the carrier here is a humble tray, and BA is simply two letters that open up to hold E and TRAY.
explanation.definitionFit: A noun-for-noun synonym: selling out your side for gain is the classic act of treachery.

clue.text: I intend boarding British Eastern aircraft

indicators.note: to board is to get on or into something

explanation.surface: A traveller announces they plan to board a British plane heading east.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I intend boarding' reads as one traveller's plan, but it splits into I, PLAN and the instruction to put them inside B and E.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by class: the two-winged machine of early flight is one kind of aircraft among many.

clue.text: What could go to making Keith musical

definitions.text: What could go to making Keith musical

parts.words: What could go to making Keith
parts.note: the surface asks what ingredients produce a man named Keith, and the letters T, H, E, K and I are those ingredients
tacked on as if Keith were musical, it tells you the answer is a stage show

explanation.surface: Someone asks what went into making a man called Keith.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue runs backwards: THE plus K (king) plus I are exactly the letters of KEITH, so 'the king and I' is what could go to making him.
explanation.definitionFit: The Rodgers and Hammerstein show set at the court of Siam is a musical, and its title is literally the letters that anagram to Keith.

clue.text: What can go off in the style of jolly telephone call

parts.note: à la = in the style of
a jolly is a Royal Marine, RM
'give me a bell' = give me a phone call

explanation.surface: A cheerful phone call that could set something off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jolly' looks like an adjective for the call; it is a noun, old slang for a Royal Marine. 'Give someone a bell' is British for phoning them.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by description: 'go off' is what alarms, bombs and guns do, and a ringing bell sounding a warning is one of them.

clue.text: Confession of bent Camden Town geek in possession of pounds

indicators.note: bent means twisted out of shape, so the letters are rearranged
whoever is in possession of something holds it

parts.note: L = pounds, from the Latin libra

explanation.surface: A crooked nerd from Camden Town, caught with money, makes a confession.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bent' reads as crooked, as in corrupt, which suits a confession; here it means the letters are twisted. Camden Town is a district of north London.
explanation.definitionFit: A near synonym: owning up that something is true is both admitting it and confessing it.

clue.text: Surf tops end of promenade

parts.note: the brows are the tops, as of hills

indicators.note: the end of a word is its last letter

explanation.surface: Waves break over the far end of a seaside promenade.
explanation.walkthrough: Surf and promenade set a seaside scene, but 'Surf' is the internet verb and 'tops' is a noun, the brows of hills.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the internet sense: surfing and browsing both mean moving idly from page to page online.

clue.text: Give way about char being suggestive

indicators.note: to go about something is to surround it

parts.note: to relent is to give way
to char is to do housework, to do for someone

explanation.surface: Someone backs down about some burning or tea while hinting at more.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Char' suggests burning or a cup of tea; here it is the verb for cleaning house, which a British cleaner also calls doing. A char is a cleaning lady.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, usually followed by 'of': a scene that strongly evokes another time or place is said to be this.

clue.text: Uppity youngster with trendier small one asleep

parts.note: S = small, as on clothing labels

explanation.surface: A cheeky young person arrives with a cooler friend and a little one who has nodded off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'With' sits in the surface as a joining word, but it is doing work: W is its standard abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: A dictionary gloss: the old-fashioned word for a cheeky, presumptuous young person.

clue.text: Fair number going topless passed

indicators.note: a word going topless loses its first letter

parts.note: SEVEN without its top letter S

explanation.surface: A number of people went topless at the fair and the moment passed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fair' pretends to be a funfair or festival; it is the adjective meaning just. The number is SEVEN, a guess the letter count confirms.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a referee who treats both sides alike, with no favourites, is fair.

clue.text: Reinstate trees damaged outside gate

indicators.note: damaged letters are knocked out of order

parts.note: an OR gate, from logic circuits

explanation.surface: Someone plans to put back trees that were damaged outside a gate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gate' is a garden gate in the surface; in the wordplay it is an electronic logic gate, and the one called OR supplies the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym as verbs: bringing something back to its former position or condition.

clue.text: Primarily a copy in likeness possessing eerie resemblance — straight up!

definitions.text: Primarily a copy in likeness possessing eerie resemblance — straight up!

indicators.note: primarily means first of all, so take each word's first letter
in a down clue, going up reads the letters backwards

parts.words: a copy in likeness possessing eerie resemblance
parts.note: the first letters of a, copy, in, likeness, possessing, eerie, resemblance

explanation.surface: An exclamation that a copy is so eerily lifelike it is uncanny, honestly.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both definition and wordplay: it describes a replica, and its initials spell one upwards. 'Straight up!' reads as 'honestly!', British slang, before it means up the column.
explanation.definitionFit: As an &lit the whole clue reads straight: a replica is exactly a copy whose likeness to the original is uncannily close.

clue.text: More than one wrong about uranium cavity

indicators.note: one word goes about, around, the other

parts.note: U is the chemical symbol for uranium

explanation.surface: Several mistakes made about a uranium-filled cavity.
explanation.walkthrough: 'More than one' tells you the wrong is plural, SINS, and U slips in before the final S.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by class: the air-filled hollows in the skull behind the nose are anatomical cavities.

clue.text: Dogmatic old wing nowadays penning extremes of twaddle

indicators.note: to pen something in is to enclose it
a word's extremes are its first and last letters

parts.note: a pinion is a bird's wing
AD, anno Domini, is our present era

explanation.surface: A pig-headed veteran of some political wing now spouts nonsense.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wing' pulls toward politics, and 'old wing' toward a faction; the wing is a bird's pinion. AD, the era we live in, is the crossword's usual nowadays.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: someone who lays down their views as beyond question is dogmatic.

clue.text: Watches lecture — it's on crab

explanation.surface: Someone sits through a lecture about crabs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Watches' reads as the audience watching the lecture, and 'on crab' as its subject, when it is where the eyestalk grows.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by location: a crab's eyes are carried on movable stalks sticking up from its shell.

clue.text: Stare at search on the internet without leave

parts.note: to google is to search online

explanation.surface: Someone looks up a person online while skiving off work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leave' looks like a holiday from work, the noun; it is the verb, GO, removed from GOOGLE.
explanation.definitionFit: A near synonym: to eye someone greedily, usually with lecherous intent.

clue.text: Homework — a chunk exhausted senior already covered

parts.note: prep is British school slang for homework

indicators.note: an exhausted word is emptied out, leaving only its outer letters

explanation.surface: An exhausted older pupil has already done a big chunk of homework.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Exhausted' reads as the tired senior; it applies to 'chunk', which is drained of HUN. Prep is homework at British schools.
explanation.definitionFit: A literal gloss: goods wrapped at the factory are covered before they reach the shop.

clue.text: Popular core to next seriously thoughtful budget

indicators.note: a word's core is its middle letters

explanation.surface: A popular thinker sets out a serious plan for the next budget.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Budget' looks like the government's annual statement, a noun; it is the adjective, as in a budget airline.
explanation.definitionFit: An adjectival sense: a budget airline or hotel is a cheap one.

clue.text: Accepted proposition advanced by Isle of Man

parts.note: A = advanced, as in A level
× is read 'by', as in a room 3 × 4
IOM is the abbreviation for the Isle of Man

explanation.surface: A proposal put forward by the Isle of Man is accepted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'By' seems a mere link, but it is the multiplication sign, X. The Isle of Man is a self-governing island in the Irish Sea.
explanation.definitionFit: A dictionary gloss: in logic, a statement taken as true without proof, the starting point for reasoning.

clue.text: Partly cover remaining drink

parts.note: to lap is to drink, as a cat does

explanation.surface: Someone half covers the rest of their drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drink' reads as a noun in the surface; it is the verb, lapping milk.
explanation.definitionFit: A literal gloss: roof tiles laid so each extends over part of the next do exactly this.

clue.text: Rough punishment of hard character to a tee?

parts.note: an air is a character or manner
a tee is a T-shirt, and the question mark flags the example

explanation.surface: Harsh treatment that suits a tough person perfectly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'To a tee' means exactly, and the surface leans on that; split off, 'a tee' is a shirt. The hair shirt was a coarse garment worn as penance.
explanation.definitionFit: Literal and figurative at once: the coarse garment of penitents was punishment you wore, and rough to the skin.

clue.text: What can reproduce staggering hundred with leg repeated?

indicators.note: letters that stagger are thrown about

explanation.surface: A staggering centipede with a hundred legs, one after another.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Staggering' seems to mean astonishing; it is the instruction to jumble C, LEG and LEG again.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by function: the female gamete, the ovum, is the cell from which new life develops.

clue.text: In-your-face prisoner, loud, going round trapping some number

indicators.note: what traps something holds it inside

parts.note: N stands for an unspecified number

explanation.surface: An aggressive inmate goes around shouting and grabbing some of the others.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Some number' is not a crowd of fellow prisoners but N, the algebra letter for any number.
explanation.definitionFit: A colloquial synonym: in-your-face behaviour is aggressive and seeks out conflict.

clue.text: What may be caught, comparatively lengthy, putting out line?

indicators.note: putting something out removes it

parts.note: L = line, which comes out of LONGER

explanation.surface: An angler asks what might be landed on a longer line cast out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Caught' is in the definition and also gives C, so the definition and wordplay overlap; the question mark admits it. 'Putting out line' sounds like fishing but deletes L.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the large sea eel is a prize for sea anglers, one of many things that may be caught.

clue.text: Say in cold seasons when coat is off one?

indicators.note: a word with its coat off loses its outer letters

parts.words: cold seasons when coat is off
parts.note: WINTERS without its outer letters W and S

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a coat can come off in the cold months.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark marks 'one' as an example, since one is just one integer among many. 'Say' is the usual signal for EG.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example, flagged by the question mark: one is a whole number, as are two and minus three.

clue.text: Deciding trick, key in writing things like this

indicators.note: 'key in writing' puts the key inside the word for writing, as one thing placed in another

parts.note: writing clues, like the one you are reading

explanation.surface: A setter explains the trick that clinches a puzzle clue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Things like this' points at the clue itself: writing them is cluing. 'Key' is a note, D, not a thing that opens locks.
explanation.definitionFit: Adjectival synonyms: the deciding game of a series is the final one that settles it.

clue.text: Conservative mess losing millions — hold tight

indicators.note: a word losing a letter has it removed

parts.note: M = millions, taken out of MUDDLE

explanation.surface: A Tory in a financial mess after losing millions is told to hang on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hold tight' sounds like advice to a politician in trouble; it is the embrace.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym as verbs: an embrace is holding someone close and tight.

clue.text: Have in mind fashionable number, band's last

indicators.note: the last of a word is its final letter

explanation.surface: A band plans to finish with a trendy number.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Number' in a band's set is a song; here it is a numeral, TEN.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: having a plan in mind is meaning to carry it out.

clue.text: Wife misled badly over moderate fungal infection

parts.note: 'my old Dutch' is Cockney for my wife

indicators.note: letters treated badly are knocked out of order

parts.note: to ease is to moderate, soften

explanation.surface: A wife badly misled about a mild fungal infection.
explanation.walkthrough: DUTCH for wife is Cockney, short for 'duchess of Fife', rhyming slang for wife. Dutch elm disease is a fungus that killed most of Britain's elms.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by class: the blight spread by bark beetles that killed most of Britain's elms is caused by a fungus.

clue.text: Carry little child with little energy

parts.note: a tot is a small child

explanation.surface: A parent too tired to carry the toddler.
explanation.walkthrough: The two 'little's work differently: the first describes the child, the second tells you to shorten energy to E.
explanation.definitionFit: An informal synonym, as in a tote bag: to lug something about with you.

clue.text: Superior canal ends in redesign with Trent

indicators.note: letters in redesign are put together a new way

explanation.surface: A fine canal comes to its end in a new scheme with the River Trent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Canal ends' begs to be read as the first and last letters of canal, C and L; all nine letters are fodder. The Trent is a major English river.
explanation.definitionFit: A dictionary sense: rising above ordinary experience, and so superior to it.

clue.text: Speculate, very involved in current home

indicators.note: what is involved in something is caught up inside it

parts.note: I is the symbol for electric current

explanation.surface: Someone speculates that they are heavily involved in their present house.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Current home' reads as where you live now; 'current' is I, from physics, and V goes inside NEST.
explanation.definitionFit: A loose synonym: putting money into shares in hope of profit is speculating, if more cautiously.

clue.text: Message on cleaner paper

parts.note: a daily is a cleaner who comes in each day
to telegraph is to send a message

explanation.surface: A note left on some kitchen roll for the cleaner.
explanation.walkthrough: In an across clue 'on' puts the message after the cleaner. A daily is British for a cleaning lady; the Daily Telegraph is a London newspaper.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the London broadsheet is one paper among many.

clue.text: Unknown island tree — one bearing fruit?

explanation.surface: A mysterious tree on an island, wondered at for its fruit.
explanation.walkthrough: The elder really does bear fruit, elderberries, so the surface is one tree seen twice.
explanation.definitionFit: A made-up agent noun, hence the question mark: a fruiting tree yields a crop, so it is one that yields.

clue.text: Note canid put back in native genus of mammals once

indicators.note: put back means turned round
'in native' places the note and the turned canid inside the word for a native, as passengers sit in a car

parts.note: a native son, someone born in a place
te is a note of the sol-fa scale

explanation.surface: A zoologist writes a note about a wild dog returned to a native genus.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Once' tells you the genus is extinct, which fits a fossil elephant. 'Put back' reverses only the canid, not the note before it; a native son is someone born in a place.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by class: the extinct elephant relatives of Asia form a genus, and 'once' marks them as gone.

clue.text: Drive off short period after I'd got up

indicators.note: in a down clue, getting up means reading upwards
a short word loses its last letter

parts.note: SPELL cut short by one letter

explanation.surface: Someone chases a thing away for a while after getting out of bed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Got up' reads as rising from bed; in a down clue it is the instruction to read upwards. The apostrophe in I'd is ignored, as punctuation always may be.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym as verbs: fears, doubts and fog are all driven away this way.

clue.text: Itemise at the outset every new expense recorded for auditor

indicators.note: the outset of each word is its first letter

parts.note: the first letters of every, new, expense, recorded

explanation.surface: An accountant lists every new expense for the auditor.
explanation.walkthrough: The accounting surface leads to reading 'auditor' as a checker of books; it means a hearer, from the Latin audire, to hear.
explanation.definitionFit: An older sense of the word: from Latin audire, to hear, an auditor was first a hearer.

clue.text: Imported plant, a form of Asian Tulipa

indicators.note: a form of something is a version of it, so the letters are reshaped

explanation.surface: A plant brought in from abroad, a sort of Asian tulip.
explanation.walkthrough: Tulipa is the botanical name for tulips, so the surface looks like a real classification. Saintpaulia is the African violet, a common houseplant.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by origin: the African violet is an East African native grown as a houseplant elsewhere, so it is imported.

clue.text: Not simple to make out messy pile behind acre

indicators.note: messy letters are in disorder

explanation.surface: A junk heap behind the field is hard to make out.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface pictures a heap of junk behind a field, and the fourteen letters of 'pile behind acre' are the whole answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain gloss: a scrawl too hard to read or decode is exactly what the phrase describes.

clue.text: Joint on dish which is tough to cut through

definitions.text: which is tough to cut through

parts.note: a breast is a joint of meat

explanation.surface: A roast served on a dish is too tough to carve.
explanation.walkthrough: The carving surface makes 'tough to cut through' sound like chewy meat; it describes armour.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by function: chest armour exists to stop a blade getting through.

clue.text: Insubstantial rowing boat stopping in awkward slews

indicators.note: to stop in a place is to stay inside it
awkward letters are ungainly, out of order

parts.note: an eight is a racing boat with eight rowers

explanation.surface: A flimsy rowing boat stays put while turning clumsily.
explanation.walkthrough: The anagram of SLEWS is W…LESS, and EIGHT fills the gap. An eight is a boat rowed by eight, as in the Oxford and Cambridge Boat Race.
explanation.definitionFit: A near synonym: something with no heft, like a feather or a ghost, is insubstantial.

clue.text: Attempt securing win's ending in tie

indicators.note: to secure something is to hold it fast inside
a word's ending is its last letter

explanation.surface: A bid to secure victory ends in a draw.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tie' is a drawn match in the surface, a noun; it is the verb, to fasten.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym as verbs: fastening with rope or cord.

clue.text: Channel fish eating what's offered by both French and Brits?

indicators.note: what eats something takes it inside

parts.note: the tench is a freshwater fish

parts.words: what's offered by both French and Brits?
parts.note: R is the one letter that FRENCH and BRITS share

explanation.surface: A fish crosses the Channel, eating something both the French and the British serve.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Channel' and 'French and Brits' conjure the English Channel; it is a plain channel, a trench. The question mark flags that 'what both offer' is a letter they have in common.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a long narrow ditch dug in the ground is a channel.

clue.text: Sparkling beers a bit after work

indicators.note: after sends the beers and the bit second, behind the work

parts.note: a cent is a small coin, a bit of money

explanation.surface: A few fizzy beers after work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sparkling' reads as describing the beers, as fizz; it means shimmering like opal. Op., short for opus, is how musical works are numbered.
explanation.definitionFit: A loose synonym: shimmering with shifting colours, as an opal does, is a kind of sparkle.

clue.text: Might I put in drained herb?

indicators.note: what is put in something goes inside it

parts.note: the arm of the law is its might, its power

explanation.surface: A cook wonders whether to add a certain herb to the drained vegetables.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Might I' opens like a polite question; 'Might' is a noun, power, and ARM I goes into SPENT.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by class: the common garden mint used in sauces and gum is a herb.

clue.text: Pardoned robber group trapped in pubs

indicators.note: what is trapped in something is held inside it

explanation.surface: A freed thief and his gang are cornered in the pubs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Group' reads as the robber's gang; it is a pop group, ABBA.
explanation.definitionFit: A biblical description: in the Gospels, the crowd chose to free this robber instead of Jesus.

clue.text: One managing the show for leader supported by king

indicators.note: in a down clue, what is supported by something sits on top of it

parts.note: Il Duce, 'the leader', was Mussolini's title

explanation.surface: A stand-in manager is backed by the king.
explanation.walkthrough: 'For leader' reads as 'standing in for the leader', which suits someone running the show; the two words work separately. Mussolini's title is a crossword favourite.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by job description: in theatre and film, this person runs the business side of the show.

clue.text: Law official initially returned for Georgia?

definitions.text: Law official initially returned for Georgia?

parts.note: the surface offers a lawyer or officer sent back to the state of Georgia
the official's initials, turned round, are the US postal code for Georgia

explanation.surface: A lawyer comes back to Georgia.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue runs backwards: an attorney general is AG by initials, and AG returned gives GA, the US abbreviation for Georgia.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by office: the chief legal adviser to a government is a law official, and one is known by the initials AG.

clue.text: Easy to see identification during incident

indicators.note: what happens during something sits inside it

explanation.surface: An ID is shown plainly at the scene of an incident.
explanation.walkthrough: The police-report surface hides a simple insertion of ID into EVENT.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: something obvious to anyone looking is easy to see.

clue.text: Improve look of casual ship's officer returning after days

indicators.note: a returning word comes back the other way

parts.note: pusser is informal naval slang for a purser

explanation.surface: A scruffy ship's officer, back after some days at sea, smartens up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Casual' reads as dressed-down, suiting the definition; it means the officer's informal name, PUSSER for purser.
explanation.definitionFit: A phrasal-verb synonym: adorning a plain thing so it looks more attractive.

clue.text: Author with depression is undecided

parts.note: to pen is to author, write
a dent is a depression in a surface

explanation.surface: A depressed writer can't make up their mind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Depression' reads as the writer's mood; it is a hollow, a DENT.
explanation.definitionFit: A rare legal sense, like pending: a case still awaiting settlement is undecided.

clue.text: One looking at body tats Naomi's sporting

indicators.note: sporting letters play about

explanation.surface: Someone eyes the tattoos Naomi is showing off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sporting' reads as wearing, showing off tattoos; it is the anagram instruction. Tats is slang for tattoos.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by job description: a scientist of bodily structure spends the working day examining bodies.

clue.text: Elevated light railroad in the US, or one above that

indicators.note: in a down clue, what is above something is written before it

parts.note: the el is an elevated railway in US cities

explanation.surface: A description of an elevated railway in America, with something above it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Elevated' looks as though it describes the railroad, the el; it belongs to the definition. In a down clue 'above that' puts OR I over EL.
explanation.definitionFit: Light is an old word for window: this bay window projects from an upper storey, so it is elevated.

clue.text: Interminable missing mates when Friday's wiped out

indicators.note: what is wiped out is removed

parts.note: the first three letters of Friday, as on a calendar

explanation.surface: A lonely stretch feels endless once Friday is wiped out.
explanation.walkthrough: Mates is British for friends, so 'missing mates' is FRIENDLESS, and removing FRI leaves ENDLESS.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: something interminable seems never to reach its end.

clue.text: Sea eagle found in Alderney

indicators.note: the answer is found inside the next word

parts.note: the four letters sit in the middle of the island's name, after its first three

explanation.surface: A sea eagle has been spotted on Alderney.
explanation.walkthrough: Alderney is one of the Channel Islands, which makes a sea eagle there plausible.
explanation.definitionFit: A crossword-regular bird: the white-tailed eagle of northern coasts, which crosswords call by this old name far more than birders do.

clue.text: Mature exercise taken in runs home

indicators.note: what is taken in goes inside

explanation.surface: An older athlete goes for a jog and runs home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Runs home' reads as a jogger heading back; it is two cricket-flavoured abbreviations side by side, R for runs and 'in' for at home.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym as verbs: fruit and cheese mature by growing ready over time.

clue.text: Earl left cross beset by crooked militant

indicators.note: what is beset by something is surrounded by it

parts.note: a liger is a cross between a lion and a tigress

explanation.surface: An angry nobleman is surrounded by corrupt militants.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cross' reads as angry, which suits an aggressive earl; it is a noun, a hybrid animal. 'Crooked' is the container, not an anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A near synonym: spoiling for a fight and aggressively combative.

clue.text: It can mean to corrupt

indicators.note: corrupted letters are spoiled, rearranged

explanation.surface: A dictionary-style note that a word can mean to corrupt.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads as a plain definition, and it is one; it is also an instruction to corrupt the letters of 'It can mean to'.
explanation.definitionFit: As an &lit the clue reads straight: one sense of the verb in any dictionary is to make impure, to corrupt.

clue.text: Ayatollahs backed for 70 per cent growth

indicators.note: backed means turned back to front
only seven of the ten letters are used

explanation.surface: Iran's religious leaders back a plan for 70 per cent growth.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads like an economic target; 'growth' is something grown, a vegetable.
explanation.definitionFit: A loose definition by example: the small mild onion is something grown, a growth of the vegetable plot.

clue.text: Hot and humid outcome that's not concerning railway

explanation.surface: A muggy day brings a verdict that has nothing to do with the railway.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not concerning railway' seems to be one phrase; 'not concerning' deletes RE, and RY is then added.
explanation.definitionFit: A weather word: a close, oppressive day with heavy damp heat is described this way.

clue.text: Live and aware broadcast that is not lacking heart

indicators.note: a word lacking its heart loses its middle letter

parts.note: NOT without its middle letter O

explanation.surface: A live broadcast that is anything but heartless.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Live' reads as a live broadcast, but belongs to the definition, living. 'Not lacking heart' reads as having heart; it is NOT with its middle removed.
explanation.definitionFit: A dictionary gloss: a creature able to feel and perceive is alive and aware.
